settings.title: We are a small studio that believes good design is clear, useful and a little unexpected.

settings.editor:
Studio Mono started in a shared room in Kreuzberg with two designers and one client. We have grown slowly and stayed independent, so we can choose projects we believe in and give them our full attention.

Today we are twelve people working across brand, digital, space and motion — one team, one studio, no departments.

posts.title: Why we still start every identity with type
posts.excerpt: Logos get the attention, but letters do the work. Our first week on any brand is spent choosing, testing and sometimes drawing type.
posts.content:
Clients often expect the first presentation to be about logos. Ours is almost always about type. A typeface carries a brand across thousands of touchpoints; the logo appears on a handful.

Test in context, not in specimens

We set real content — an invoice, a push notification, a sign over a door — in four or five candidates. The right choice is usually obvious within an afternoon.

  • Does it hold up at 11 pixels and at 11 metres?
  • Does it have the languages you need, including the ones planned for next year?
  • Can your team license it everywhere it will be used?

A brand is mostly words. Choose the letters before you choose anything else.

Jonas Weber

Only once the type is settled do we draw the mark. It almost always gets simpler as a result.

posts.title: Grids are a promise, not a cage
posts.excerpt: A good grid makes the hundred small decisions in a layout for you, so you can spend your energy on the three that matter.
posts.content:
Every project we deliver includes a layout grid. Not because we love rules, but because grids let a team of twenty make pages that look like one person made them.

Fewer columns than you think

We usually start with a twelve-column grid and end with six. Fewer columns make for bolder layouts and simpler responsive behaviour.

Break it on purpose

The most memorable pages break the grid once, deliberately. The grid is what makes the break visible.

posts.title: What we learned designing for a bank
posts.excerpt: Eighteen months with Atlas Bank taught us about trust, regulation and why the boring screens are the most important ones.
posts.content:
When Atlas asked us to rebuild their brand and app, we expected the hard part to be the visual identity. It turned out to be the confirmation screens.

Trust lives in the details

People decide whether to trust a bank in moments of anxiety: a failed payment, a blocked card, a large transfer. We designed those screens first and the marketing site last.

  1. Plain language, reviewed by compliance from week one
  2. One primary action per screen, always in the same place
  3. A calm colour for errors — never red alone

The best compliment we got was that the new app felt boring. In banking, that means safe.

Eighteen months on, support calls about payments are down by a third.

posts.title: Our process, in four honest steps
posts.excerpt: Listen, make, test, look after. What actually happens between the first call and the launch party — including the messy middle.
posts.content:
Every studio has a process diagram. Ours has four circles, and like everyone else’s it is tidier than reality. Here is what really happens.

1. Listen

A week of interviews with your team, your customers and sometimes your competitors’ customers. We write a two-page brief and agree on it before designing anything.

2. Make

Two weeks to real prototypes. Expect rough edges and strong opinions.

3. Test

We put the work in front of people early and change our minds often. The messy middle is where the good ideas come from.

4. Look after

Launch is the start. We stay on for at least three months to refine the system with your team.

posts.title: How to write a design brief we will love
posts.excerpt: You do not need a forty-page document. One page, five questions and an honest budget will get you a better project.
posts.content:
We read a lot of briefs. The best ones are short, specific and honest about constraints. Here is the template we send to new clients.

  1. What are you making, and for whom?
  2. What should people think, feel or do differently afterwards?
  3. What must not change?
  4. When does it need to be ready, and why then?
  5. What is the budget range?

That last question makes people nervous. It should not: a budget is a design constraint like any other, and knowing it lets us propose the right scope instead of guessing.

A one-page brief with a real budget beats a forty-page brief with none.
